title: Registration uniqueness check is a TOCTOU: two concurrent sign-ups with the same username create two Keycloak users and surface a raw constraint violation instead of a conflict
actual: register() calls validateUniqueConstraints() (existsByUsername / existsByEmail / existsByPhone), then creates the Keycloak user, then inserts the local row. The checks are not atomic with the insert, so two concurrent registrations with the same username both pass the check and both create a Keycloak user. The local insert then fails on the unique index and the catch rolls the Keycloak user back - but the caller receives the raw DataIntegrityViolationException (HTTP 500) instead of the catalogue's AUTH_USERNAME_EXISTS conflict.
expected: A duplicate registration returns AUTH_USERNAME_EXISTS, and at most one Keycloak user is created.
trigger: A double-clicked sign-up form, or two browser tabs submitting the same registration.
root_cause: The uniqueness pre-check is not backed by a constraint-violation mapping, unlike the equivalent fix applied to the promotion reservation (F-047).
consequences: HTTP 500 instead of 409 for a normal business conflict; the compensating Keycloak delete is a best-effort call that can itself fail, leaving an orphan Keycloak user with the same username.
remediation: Map the unique-constraint violation on the local insert to the catalogue conflict codes, exactly as F-047 does for the coupon reservation.
regression_test: Integration test: two concurrent registrations with the same username must yield one success and one AUTH_USERNAME_EXISTS, and exactly one Keycloak user must survive.

title: A password change did not revoke the sessions established with the old password
actual: changePassword() called keycloakAdminClient.resetUserPassword(...) and returned. Keycloak's admin reset-password endpoint changes the credential but does NOT end the user's existing sessions, so every refresh token issued before the change stayed valid. The same applied to resetPassword(). KeycloakAdminClient already had the /logout admin call for disableUser(), but the credential-change paths never used it.
expected: A credential change revokes the sessions established with the old credential, so a captured refresh token cannot outlive the password it was issued against.
trigger: A password change or reset - most importantly a reset performed because the password may have been compromised.
root_cause: The admin client's reset-password flow was implemented without the accompanying session revocation.
consequences: An attacker holding a stolen refresh token keeps full access to the account even after the owner changes the password or resets it after a breach. This is the standard session-invalidation-on-credential-change control (OWASP ASVS V2 session management).
remediation: Add KeycloakAdminClient.logoutUser(userId) (POST /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{id}/logout) and call it after every credential change. The revocation is best-effort: the credential change has already been applied, so a revocation failure is logged at ERROR rather than reported as a failed password change.
regression_test: auth-service: changePasswordVerifiesOldPasswordThenResets asserts logoutUser is called; changePasswordSucceedsEvenWhenSessionRevocationFails asserts a revocation failure does not turn the change into an error.
remediation_applied: KeycloakAdminClient.logoutUser added; UserServiceImpl.changePassword and resetPassword both call revokeSessions(...) after the credential change.
verification_evidence: auth-service module green (33 tests) including the two new revocation assertions.

title: A password reset did not revoke the sessions established with the compromised password
actual: resetPassword() called keycloakAdminClient.resetUserPassword(...) and marked the reset token used, without revoking the user's existing Keycloak sessions. A reset is the operation an account owner performs precisely because the password may have leaked, so the surviving sessions are the exact sessions that must die.
expected: Resetting a password revokes every session and refresh token issued under the old password.
trigger: A password reset following a suspected compromise.
root_cause: Same root cause as F-051 - the credential-change path omitted the session revocation.
consequences: The compromised session survives the remediation the owner performed to end it.
remediation: Covered by the same revokeSessions(...) call added for F-051.
regression_test: auth-service: the resetPassword test asserts logoutUser is called for the reset user.
remediation_applied: UserServiceImpl.resetPassword calls revokeSessions(user.getKeycloakUserId()) after the credential change.

title: The password reset token has no version column: a reset token can be redeemed twice concurrently
actual: PasswordResetToken has a 'used' flag but no @Version. resetPassword() loads the token with findByTokenHashAndUsedFalse, changes the Keycloak password, then sets used=true and saves. Two concurrent redemptions of the same token both read used=false and both change the password; the last writer wins and the first password is silently replaced.
expected: A reset token is single-use even under concurrent redemption.
trigger: A reset link is opened twice, or an attacker races the legitimate owner.
root_cause: The consume step is a read-modify-write without a version guard or a conditional UPDATE.
consequences: The token can be used twice; the second use overwrites the password the owner just set, so the owner's chosen password is lost without any error.
remediation: Consume the token with a conditional UPDATE (UPDATE ... SET used = true WHERE token_hash = ? AND used = false) and only proceed when it affected one row; add a version column for the same reason as F-011 / F-044.
regression_test: Concurrency test: two concurrent redemptions of the same token must produce exactly one password change and one rejection.

title: The password reset email is never sent - the only PasswordResetEmailSender implementation logs instead of dispatching, so the reset flow cannot complete
actual: PasswordResetEmailSender is a port with exactly one implementation, DefaultPasswordResetEmailSender, whose sendResetEmail() body is a log.info line. forgotPassword() persists a reset token, calls the sender and reports success - so the API answers 'a password reset instruction has been sent' while no message ever leaves the process. The raw token is correctly NOT logged, so there is no leak; the flow is simply non-functional.
expected: The reset token reaches the user over the notification channel (notification-service already has an SMTP sender).
trigger: Any forgot-password request in a real deployment.
root_cause: The seam was created but no SMTP-backed implementation was wired.
consequences: Users cannot recover a forgotten password; the endpoint reports success, so the failure is invisible to operators and to the caller. Support load is the only signal.
remediation: Implement the sender on top of notification-service's SMTP channel (or a JavaMailSender), and fail the endpoint when the dispatch fails so the caller is not told a message was sent when it was not.
regression_test: Integration test: forgot-password must invoke a sender that records the delivery, and the reset link must work end to end.

title: A self-registration naming only privileged roles created an account with ZERO realm roles - the user could sign in but every authorization rule failed
actual: extractRoles() returned the USER fallback only when the request omitted the roles field entirely. When the request named a non-allowed role ({"ADMIN"}, {"ADMIN","SERVICE","MANAGER"}, ...) the whitelist filter removed every entry and the resulting EMPTY list was used for BOTH the Keycloak role assignment (createUser) and the local user_role rows. The pre-existing test registerAllDisallowedRolesResultsInEmptyList ASSERTED this behaviour, so the defect was locked in by its own specification.
expected: The whitelist exists to stop a self-registration obtaining a privileged role - not to strip the customer of their base role. A registration must always end up with at least USER.
trigger: A client that sends a roles field containing only privileged names (the field is deprecated but still accepted and bound).
root_cause: The fallback was applied to the pre-filter list instead of the post-filter list.
consequences: The account is created in Keycloak with no realm role and in the local database with no role row. The customer can authenticate, but every @PreAuthorize rule fails, and every @PreAuthorize-based endpoint returns 403 for an account that the registration flow reported as created. Recovering it requires an operator.
remediation: Apply the USER fallback to the POST-filter list, so an empty filtered result falls back to USER. The test was updated to assert the corrected behaviour (and renamed accordingly).
regression_test: auth-service: registerAllDisallowedRolesFallsBackToUser asserts Keycloak receives ["USER"] and the local DB receives the USER role row, and that the empty-role call never happens.
remediation_applied: UserServiceImpl.extractRoles now falls back to USER when the whitelist filter empties the list.
verification_evidence: auth-service module green (33 tests) with the corrected test.

title: The local role catalogue (USER, PM, ADMIN) does not match the provisioned Keycloak realm roles (ADMIN, USER, MANAGER, SERVICE)
actual: RoleName declares USER, PM and ADMIN, while the Keycloak realm ships ADMIN, USER, MANAGER and SERVICE. RoleMapper.toRoleName maps an unknown name to BusinessException.badRequest("auth.unsupported.role"), so the mismatch is handled cleanly at the API boundary - assigning MANAGER or SERVICE through /api/v1/roles returns a 400 with a clear code rather than an unmapped exception. The local catalogue is nevertheless a subset with one invented role (PM) that does not exist in the realm.
expected: The local role catalogue and the realm's realm roles stay in step.
trigger: An operator tries to grant MANAGER or SERVICE through the admin role API.
root_cause: The catalogue was written independently of the realm import.
consequences: The SERVICE role - which every service-to-service call depends on - cannot be managed through the auth-service admin API; MANAGER cannot be granted either. The mismatch is fail-closed (400) rather than dangerous.
remediation: Align RoleName with the realm (add MANAGER and SERVICE, or drop PM), or generate the catalogue from the realm at startup.
regression_test: Contract test asserting that every RoleName constant exists as a realm role in docker/keycloak/import/ecommerce-realm.json.

title: forgotPassword logs the email address of a non-existent account
actual: forgotPassword() returns the same generic message for every input (no user enumeration through the API - that part is correct), but it logs 'Password reset requested for non-existent email: {}' with the submitted address, while the existing-account branch logs the username. The log therefore becomes a list of addresses that do not belong to the platform.
expected: Logs do not accumulate third-party email addresses. A single indistinguishable log line per request is enough to drive an operational alert.
trigger: Any forgot-password request for an address that is not registered.
root_cause: The two branches log at different granularity.
consequences: The log stream becomes a soft user-enumeration oracle for anyone with log access, and it accumulates personal data about unrelated people.
remediation: Log one indistinguishable line per request (optionally with a hash of the address) and raise a counter for the not-found case so an enumeration attempt is still visible to monitoring.
regression_test: Unit test: the two branches produce the same log shape (no raw address for the not-found case).
